documents.section_title: From zero to your first event, in about five minutes
documents.title: From zero to your first event, in about five minutes
documents.content:
1. Quickstart

 

## From zero to your first event, in about five minutes

 

Ravensight is hosted. You do not run a server, you point your game at ours.

 

1. **Create an account.** Sign in at `https://app.ravensight.io` through RealitySE, the identity system Ravensight runs on. Use email and password, or one of the SSO providers: Apple, Google, Facebook, GitHub, Twitch, Xbox, or Steam.
 
1. **Create a project.** A project is one title, and it holds one game per environment. The first time you sign in the dashboard asks for a name, an id and an engine, and creates the project with its production environment in one step. Every feature is available right away, no upgrade required. See [Projects and environments](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#projects) for the shape.
 
1. **Copy the ingest key.** Each environment has its own. It is shown once on the confirmation screen and looks like `gt_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx`. It is publishable: safe to ship inside your game binary, since it can only create sessions, read the tracking on/off switch and the AI suggestions feed, submit player reports and submit doctor reports. It cannot read analytics or manage your account. If you lose it, rotate it from **Settings > Projects** for a new one.
 
1. **Add the autoload.** Copy `Ravensight.gd` into your Godot project, e.g. `res://autoload/Ravensight.gd`. Open **Project > Project Settings > Autoload**, add the script, name it `Ravensight`, and enable it. Set `ingest_key` to the key from step 3 before Ravensight's `_ready()` runs: edit the default at the top of `Ravensight.gd`, or set it from an autoload listed above `Ravensight`. `api_url` already points at `https://api.ravensight.io`. Not on Godot? Install the SDK for your engine from the [SDK list](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#platform-support) instead (Unity, Unreal, web, iOS, Android, C++, Odin or LÖVE), or call the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#http-api) directly from anything else.
 
1. **Send your first event.** Call `track_event()` from anywhere in your game.
 
1. **See the dashboard.** Pick your project in the switcher, and the environment beside it if the project has more than one. The SDK sends events in batches, 5 seconds after the first one waits, so they typically show up within a few seconds, no restart needed.

 

Godot, res://autoload/ravensight.gd

 

```
Ravensight.track_event("level_completed", {
    "level": 3,
    "score": 15000,
    "time_seconds": 87.4
})
```

 

**Not on Godot?** The same account and ingest key work against the plain [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#http-api): three headers and a JSON body from any engine or client that can make a POST request.

documents.content:
2. Install an SDK

 

## Where the SDKs run

 

Every SDK ships as source and speaks plain HTTPS to the same four endpoints. There is no prebuilt binary in any of them. The platform specific code is small: the LÖVE SDK's HTTPS transports, and the app background handling on iOS and Android. The C++ and Odin SDKs link libcurl for the HTTP calls. The LÖVE SDK runs on the desktop, and on the web through the JavaScript SDK; see the [LÖVE SDK reference](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#love-sdk). A cell says Untested where no build of that SDK has been run on that platform yet.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Consoles
documents.content:
### Consoles

 

Nothing in any SDK is blocked on a console. What is blocked is everything else about console networking: each platform holder requires that outbound traffic, privacy disclosure, and any data collection be declared and approved as part of certification, and NDA restrictions mean we cannot ship console specific code publicly anyway. Ravensight is an ordinary HTTPS call from your title's own network stack, and passing cert with it is the developer's responsibility, exactly as it would be for a leaderboard or a patch notes fetch.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Mobile privacy
documents.content:
### Mobile privacy

 

Ravensight does not touch an advertising identifier. Every SDK generates its own random device id on first run and stores it locally. The Godot and LÖVE SDKs write 32 lowercase hex characters, a hyphen and the OS name, so `3f9ac2e17b5d4c0e8a61f2b9d7c04e5a-android` is what one looks like. The Unity, C++, Odin, iOS and Android SDKs write `dev_` and 32 hex characters from 16 random bytes; Unreal writes `dev_` and a random UUID, and the JavaScript SDK writes `dev_` and a random UUID where the browser or Node offers one, else 32 hex characters. No IDFA on iOS, no Android advertising id, no hardware identifier, and no IP based fingerprinting. That id is meaningless outside your game's own data, and nothing in Ravensight ever joins it to a name, an email or an account, because the SDK has no field for any of those.

 

An event row holds the game id, the device id, the session id, the event name, a timestamp, and the level, platform, version and payload you sent. It holds no IP address, user agent or location, and it is deleted after 90 days. Two things outlive that window: one record per game and device with the first day it was seen, kept for the game's lifetime so lifetime and new-player counts stay correct, and any feedback text a player typed, kept until you delete it or the game.

 

**No App Tracking Transparency prompt is required for Ravensight.** Apple defines tracking as linking data collected from your app about a user or device with data collected from other companies' apps, websites or offline properties for targeted advertising or advertising measurement, or sharing it with a data broker. Ravensight does neither: the id is yours alone, it is never combined with another company's data, and nothing reaches an ad network or a data broker. So on Ravensight's account you do not need to call `requestTrackingAuthorization`. If something else in your app does track across companies, that decision is unchanged by this.

 

Two SDK calls exist for studios that show their own consent screen. Ravensight ships no consent UI; wire these to your own settings menu if your audience or your lawyer wants one.

 

- **The opt-out** stops the SDK sending anything: queued events are dropped and no further request is made, not even the startup check. Every SDK except JavaScript saves the choice locally, so it survives a restart until the player turns it back on. The JavaScript SDK does not store it: keep the choice in your own settings and apply it before the first event on every launch.
 
- **The reset** saves a new random id and opens a new session under it, so a player can start a fresh analytics identity from your game's own settings. Rows already stored under the old id are not rewritten; they expire with the 90-day window, or sooner if you delete the game.

 

| SDK | Opt-out | Reset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Godot | `Ravensight.set_tracking_enabled(false)` | `Ravensight.reset_device_id()` |
| JavaScript | `rs.setEnabled(false)`, not saved | `await rs.resetDeviceId()` |
| LÖVE | `ravensight.setTrackingEnabled(false)` | `ravensight.resetDeviceId()` |
| Unity | `Ravensight.SetTrackingEnabled(false)` | `Ravensight.ResetDeviceId()` |
| Unreal | `SetTrackingEnabled(false)` on the subsystem | `ResetDeviceId()` |
| C++ | `client.set_tracking_enabled(false)` | `client.reset_device_id()` |
| Odin | `rs.set_tracking_enabled(client, false)` | `rs.reset_device_id(client)` |
| iOS | `Ravensight.setTrackingEnabled(false)` | `Ravensight.resetDeviceId()` |
| Android | `Ravensight.setTrackingEnabled(context, false)` | `Ravensight.resetDeviceId()` |

 

You do still have disclosure obligations, and they are yours rather than ours, because Apple and Google ask the publisher of record. The answers below cover what Ravensight collects on its own account; add whatever your own events carry on top, and if you send something personal, disclose it.

 

- **App Store privacy details.** Declare **Device ID** under Identifiers and **Product Interaction** under Usage Data, both under **Data Not Linked to You**, purpose **Analytics**, and answer **Data Not Used to Track You**. Add **Crash Data** under Diagnostics only if you send crash events; Ravensight has no crash reporter of its own.
 
- **Apple privacy manifest.** With any SDK other than the Swift package, add the two `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes` entries below to your `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, with `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked` false and `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking` false on both, and `NSPrivacyTracking` false. The required-reason entries depend on the SDK. The Swift package ships its own `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, which Xcode merges into your app's privacy report: it declares `NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults` with reason `CA92.1`, tracking false, and Device ID and Product Interaction as collected, so you do not add those yourself. Unity's `PlayerPrefs` is `UserDefaults` on iOS, so a Unity game's manifest must declare `NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults` with `CA92.1` if the engine's own manifest does not already. Godot and Unreal store a file in the app's own container and add no required-reason entry of their own, so leave whatever your engine's export already declares exactly as it is.
 
- **Android.** The `android.permission.INTERNET` permission is the only one any SDK needs. No `AD_ID` permission, and nothing that triggers a runtime permission dialog. In the Play Console Data safety form declare **Device or other IDs** and **App interactions** as collected, not shared, for Analytics, not for advertising; answer yes to encrypted in transit, because every request is HTTPS; and answer yes to a deletion path, which is the reset call above plus deleting the game. With the native Android SDK, merge its Auto Backup rules so the device id and the saved opt-out stay on the device rather than following the player's cloud backup to a new phone.

 

PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, the Ravensight entries

 

```
<key>NSPrivacyTracking</key>
<false/>
<key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes</key>
<array>
  <dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
    <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeDeviceID</string>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
    <array>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAnalytics</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
    <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeProductInteraction</string>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
    <array>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAnalytics</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
</array>
```

 

**What our sub-processors see**, so your "shared with third parties" answer is honest. The event stream is stored with our cloud, event database and operational database providers, who process it only to run Ravensight for you. When you use the AI analyst, the model provider receives the text a player typed into feedback and the rows and totals the analyst's tools queried, under contract; it never receives a player's report image. The embedding provider receives feedback text so you can search it. A product analytics service runs in the dashboard and on this website, never inside a game. Nothing reaches an ad network or a data broker, and nothing is sold. Both stores treat a service provider acting on your instructions as your own processing rather than sharing, which is why "not shared" is the correct answer. The [privacy policy](https://www.ravensight.io/privacy/) names every provider.

 

Ravensight itself is the processor here, not the controller. What ends up in an event payload is entirely what you chose to put there, so if you send something personal, disclose it.

 

#### What your privacy label can say

 

These are the answers for a game that uses Ravensight and nothing else that collects data. Each row says why, against the store's own definition, so you can defend it in review. Apple's rule for "not linked": direct identifiers are stripped before collection and you never try to link the data back to a person afterwards. Ravensight never collects a direct identifier in the first place, and there is no account to link to.

 

App Store privacy details

 

| Data type | Answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identifiers: Device ID | Collected. Analytics. Data Not Linked to You. Data Not Used to Track You. | A random per-install id that is never joined to a name, email or account, and never combined with another company's data, so it meets neither the "linked" test nor the tracking definition. |
| Usage Data: Product Interaction | Collected. Analytics. Data Not Linked to You. Data Not Used to Track You. | Event names, levels and session timing from your own game only, stored against the same unlinked id and used for nothing but your dashboard. |
| Diagnostics: Crash Data | Only if you send crash events. Same answers as above. | Ravensight has no crash reporter; a crash you report as an event is Product Interaction unless it carries a stack trace, in which case declare Crash Data too. |
| User Content: Other User Content | Only if you enable player feedback or Player Reports. Analytics. Not Linked. Not Used to Track. | Free text a player types and any image they attach are stored under the device id until you delete them; disclose what your players can type. |
| Contact Info, Location, Financial Info, Health, Browsing History, Search History, Purchases | Not collected. | The SDK has no field for any of these, and the privacy policy commits that it never will. |

 

Google Play Data safety

 

| Question or data type | Answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Device or other IDs | Collected. Not shared. Analytics. Not used for advertising or marketing. | The random per-install id above; it leaves your game only for Ravensight's own storage, which Play treats as your processing, not sharing. |
| App activity: App interactions | Collected. Not shared. Analytics. | Your gameplay events, under the same id, used only for your dashboard. |
| App info and performance: Crash logs | Only if you send crash events. | Ravensight has no crash reporter of its own. |
| Messages or other user-generated content | Only if you enable player feedback or Player Reports. | Text a player types is stored until you delete it and reaches the model provider for analysis under contract. |
| Is the data encrypted in transit? | Yes. | Every SDK talks to Ravensight over HTTPS only. |
| Is there a way to request deletion? | Yes. | The SDK's reset call (see the table under Mobile privacy) severs the player from their history and the old rows expire within 90 days; deleting the game removes everything at once. |
| Is collection required or optional? | Optional if you wire the SDK's opt-out call (see the table under Mobile privacy) to a setting, otherwise required. | The switch sends nothing while off, and every SDK except JavaScript saves it; Ravensight ships no consent screen, so this one is your call. |

 

For a game that runs no ads, the one sentence this lets you put on your store page, and mean it: **"No ads, no tracking, no account needed."** If you later add an ad network, an attribution SDK or a sign-in, revisit every row above, because the first two are exactly what the tracking definition is about.

### SDK repositories

 

| SDK | Status | Repository |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Godot | Stable | [ravensight-godot](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-godot) |
| JavaScript | Stable | [ravensight-js](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-js), [ravensight on npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ravensight) |
| Unity | Beta: verified in the Unity 6 Editor and a macOS player | [ravensight-unity](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unity) |
| Unreal | Beta: compiled and spec tested on Unreal Engine 5.8.3 | [ravensight-unreal](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unreal) |
| C++ | Beta | [ravensight-cpp](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-cpp) |
| Odin | Beta | [ravensight-odin](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-odin) |
| LÖVE | 0.2.0, desktop, web through the JavaScript SDK | [ravensight-love](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-love) |
| iOS | Beta | [ravensight-ios](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-ios) |
| Android | Beta | [ravensight-android](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-android) |

 

Beta means the SDK meets the same contract as the others and its own tests pass, but no released game has shipped with it yet; it becomes Stable when one does.

 

Every SDK implements the same protocol against the same four endpoints, and its batching and retry logic is tested with a fake network rather than the live API. For the 0.2.0 releases these suites were run: the Godot behaviour tests, headless on macOS and in CI; the Unity SDK's engine-free core tests in CI and, for 0.2.1, its 58 EditMode and 4 Play Mode tests in the Unity 6000.6.5f1 Editor, plus a macOS player run end to end; the Unreal plugin for 0.2.1, built on Unreal Engine 5.8.3 with warnings treated as errors, its 78 automation specs run headless in the editor, and the Mac editor and game targets built, though no packaged game has run yet; the C++ and Odin suites on macOS; the Swift package's tests on macOS and the iOS Simulator; the Android SDK's JVM and Robolectric tests; and the LÖVE SDK's suite (`luajit spec/run.lua`). Each SDK's README names the commands and toolchain versions. If your engine is not here, the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#http-api) is three headers and a JSON body.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Ravensight.gd
documents.content:
3. Godot SDK reference

 

## Ravensight.gd

 

One autoload script. It owns device identification, session creation, batching, retries, and the offline queue, so your game code only ever needs to call `track_event()`.

 

Code samples scroll horizontally when needed. Focus a sample and use the arrow keys, or swipe to read a long line.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Options
documents.content:
### Options

 

Set these before Ravensight's `_ready()` runs: edit the defaults at the top of `Ravensight.gd`, or set them from an autoload listed above `Ravensight`.

 

| Property | Type | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_url` | String | `https://api.ravensight.io` | With or without `/api/v1`, with or without a trailing slash. Empty means the default. `api_base()` returns the normalised root. |
| `ingest_key` | String | `gt_live_your_ingest_key_here` | The publishable key from your game's confirmation screen. |
| `game_version` | String | `1.0.0` | Sent with every session. |
| `enabled` | bool | `true` | `false` turns the SDK off for this run: no request of any kind, nothing queued, no `game_started`, until `set_enabled(true)`. Never saved. `set_tracking_enabled()` still saves the player's choice while it is `false`. |
| `max_queue_size` | int | `500` | Unsent events kept. The oldest are dropped first; a queued `game_started` is kept. |
| `flush_interval` | float | `5.0` | Seconds an event waits so it can go out with others. 50 waiting events go at once. |
| `handle_quit` | bool | `true` | The SDK sets `auto_accept_quit` to false, flushes on a close request (and the Android back button when `quit_on_go_back` is on), then calls `get_tree().quit()` itself within 1.5 seconds. Set false if your game has its own "really quit?" dialog; the SDK then only flushes on a close request, and your dialog calls `Ravensight.quit()`. |
| `session_timeout` | float | `1800.0` | Android and iOS only: seconds in the background after which the session counts as over. See Automatic events. |

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Public functions
documents.content:
### Public functions

 

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `track_event(event_name: String, data: Dictionary = {})` | Queue an event. It only queues: events go out in batches of up to 50, `flush_interval` seconds after the first waiting event, at once when 50 are waiting, on `flush()`, when the app goes to the background, and on quit. Safe to call from any autoload, even before Ravensight's own `_ready()`. |
| `flush()` | Send what is queued now instead of waiting for the timer. Cuts a backoff wait short; a server's Retry-After wait still holds. |
| `quit(exit_code = 0)` | Send `game_exited` and the queue, then quit. Call it from your own Quit button instead of `get_tree().quit()`. |
| `submit_feedback(message: String, category: String = "", rating: int = 0)` | Send player feedback. `category` is optional and one of `FEEDBACK_CATEGORIES`: `bug`, `suggestion`, `complaint`, `praise`, `playtest`, `other`. `rating` is 0 to leave it out, or a whole number from 1 to 5. Anything else fails at once with `invalid_category` or `invalid_rating` and no request is made. Needs an open session; unlike `track_event()`, a call made before one exists fails immediately rather than queueing. |
| `set_tracking_enabled(on: bool)` | The player's opt-out, saved across launches. See Player privacy below. |
| `is_tracking_enabled()` | `true` while events are collected: enabled, not opted out, kill switch on. |
| `reset_device_id()` | Start a fresh analytics identity for this install. Returns the new id. |
| `set_enabled(on: bool)` | The game's own switch for this run (see `enabled`). |
| `get_status_reason()` | Why nothing is being sent, or `""`. See Startup and failures. |
| `api_base()` | The API root requests go to, for example `https://api.ravensight.io/api/v1`. |
| `is_playtest()` | `true` in a run driven by the Ravensight playtest runner. |
| `set_playtest_context(ctx)` | Puts a running game into playtest mode. The SDK already does this from the playtest runner's variables, so a game never needs to call it by hand. |
| `fetch_suggestions()` | Experimental. Answers on `suggestions_received`; while tracking is off nothing is requested and it answers with an empty list. |

 

`Ravensight.tracking_enabled` is read-only and gives the same answer as `is_tracking_enabled()`. `Ravensight.session_token` is the open session's token, or `""` until one opens. If your game server should report into the player's session, hand it this token and have it send it as `joinToken` when it opens its own session (see the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#http-api)). The SDK never computes a session id itself.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Signals
documents.content:
### Signals

 

| Signal | Fires when |
| --- | --- |
| `session_ready` | A session is open. |
| `session_failed(reason: String)` | Opening a session failed: `"invalid_key"` for a refused key, otherwise the server's error code or `"offline"`. Retried for you unless the key was refused. |
| `tracking_disabled(source: String)` | `"server"` for the kill switch, `"player"` after an opt-out, `"init"` when `enabled` is `false` or after `set_enabled(false)`. |
| `status_changed(reason: String)` | `get_status_reason()` changed. |
| `events_flushed(count: int)` | A batch was accepted. `count` is the number sent, which can be more than the server stored: an event timestamped more than 90 days ago is dropped (see [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#http-api)). |
| `flush_failed(reason: String)` | A batch failed. It is retried for you, except one event the server refuses with 400, which is dropped. |
| `feedback_submitted` | Feedback was accepted. |
| `feedback_failed(reason: String)` | Feedback failed: `"disabled"`, `"empty_message"`, `"invalid_category"`, `"invalid_rating"` or `"no_session"` before sending (no request is made), or the server's error code. |
| `suggestions_received(suggestions: Array)` | Experimental. Carries the result of `fetch_suggestions()`. |
| `event_tracked(event_name: String, data: Dictionary)` | Every time `track_event()` queues an event, with the data actually queued (playtest tags included in a playtest run). Use it to mirror tracked events elsewhere in the running game. |

 

```
func _ready():
    Ravensight.session_ready.connect(func(): print("ready"))
    Ravensight.session_failed.connect(func(reason): print("session failed: ", reason))
    Ravensight.tracking_disabled.connect(func(source): print("tracking off: ", source))
    Ravensight.status_changed.connect(func(reason): print("status: ", reason))
    Ravensight.events_flushed.connect(func(count): print("sent ", count, " events"))
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Automatic events
documents.content:
### Automatic events

 

The SDK sends exactly two events by itself:

 

- **`game_started`**, once per session. It is queued at launch, first in the queue with the launch time, and sent once the kill switch check allows it. It is never queued while the SDK is disabled or the player has opted out; a game enabled later in the run queues it then, once.
 
- **`game_exited`**, once, when the game quits through `Ravensight.quit()`, or through the window close or the Android back button when the SDK handles that quit (`handle_quit`). Losing focus on a desktop is not an exit: it only sends what is queued.

 

**Android and iOS.** Going to the background tries to send what is queued and saves a small marker (`user://ravensight_bg.save`); no event is sent. Back in the foreground within 30 minutes (`session_timeout`), nothing happens. After 30 minutes or more, the old session gets `game_exited` stamped with the moment the app went to the background, and a new session starts with `game_started`. If the player swipes the app away while it is in the background, the next launch sends that `game_exited` from the marker (one attempt, before anything else) and deletes the marker.

 

**Web export.** The browser gives a Godot web game no close notification, so a web build never sends `game_exited`. `game_started` and everything you track are sent as usual.

 

From your own Quit button, call `Ravensight.quit()` instead of `get_tree().quit()`, which quits at once and sends no `game_exited`:

 

```
func _on_quit_pressed() -> void:
    Ravensight.quit()
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Startup and failures
documents.content:
### Startup and failures

 

`get_status_reason()` says why nothing is being sent, and `status_changed` fires when that changes.

 

| Reason | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `""` | Nothing is wrong: a session is open, or opening normally. |
| `disabled` | `enabled` is `false`, or the player opted out. |
| `invalid_key` | The server refused the ingest key (401, or a 403 that is not one of the codes below). Logged once as `Ravensight: ingest key refused (invalid_key), sending stopped for this run. Check your gt_live_ key.` Automatic sending stops for the run; events keep queueing and `flush()` tries once more. |
| `tracking_disabled` | The kill switch is off for your game. The queue is dropped and nothing more is sent this run. |
| `offline` | No answer (no connection, or no reply within 15 seconds). Retried after 10 seconds, doubling up to 5 minutes; events are kept. |
| `rate_limited` | The server said slow down (429, or 503 with Retry-After). The SDK waits exactly the Retry-After time. |
| `session_failed` | Opening a session failed for another reason (retried with the same backoff), or a playtest token was refused. |
| `playtest_job_closed` | The playtest job this run belongs to has closed. Nothing more is sent. |

 

If the server refuses one oversized event, the batch is halved until that event is alone, then it is dropped and reported on `flush_failed`, so it never costs the events around it. Events can be lost: the oldest go when more than `max_queue_size` are waiting, and whatever is still unsent when the game quits is not saved for the next launch.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Kill switch
documents.content:
### Kill switch

 

On boot, the SDK calls `GET /api/v1/settings` once with `ingest_key`. If tracking is off for your game, it goes idle for that run: no session is created and nothing is sent, and the `tracking_disabled` signal fires with source `"server"`. A `403 tracking_disabled` from any request has the same effect mid-run. Flip `trackingEnabled` from the dashboard's game settings and it takes effect on the game's next launch, no update required.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Levels and deaths
documents.content:
### Levels and deaths

 

Ravensight builds the level funnel, per-level deaths and journeys from your event names, with no configuration: names containing `died`, `destroyed` or `killed` count as deaths, `start`, `begin` or `enter` as level starts, and `complet`, `finish`, `win` or `clear` as completions. The `level`, `location` or `track` field says where. To say what an event means instead, set `rs_kind` in its data to `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death` or `none`. It is read before the name, and `none` opts an event out. Keys that start with `rs_` are reserved for Ravensight.

 

```
Ravensight.track_event("boss_phase_begin", {"level": "castle", "rs_kind": "none"})
Ravensight.track_event("run_over", {"level": "castle", "rs_kind": "death"})
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Player privacy
documents.content:
### Player privacy

 

The device id is 16 random bytes from the operating system's secure random source, as hex, plus the OS name, generated on first run and saved in `user://`. `set_tracking_enabled()` writes the choice at once and can be called at any time, even from an autoload that runs before Ravensight's `_ready()`, or while `enabled` is `false`. A saved opt-out wins over `enabled = true`: on the next launch nothing is sent, not even the kill switch check. Turning it off drops the queue. `reset_device_id()` saves a new random id, drops the queue and the session, and returns the new id. In a playtest run both do nothing but print one line.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Telling players
documents.content:
### Telling players

 

You do not need a permission prompt, but saying what the game sends is good manners. A paragraph your game can show, in a settings screen or on its store page:

 

This game sends anonymous gameplay events (what happens in the game, never who you are) to Ravensight so we can improve it. You can turn this off in Settings at any time.

 

And the toggle behind "turn this off":

 

```
# an "Analytics" switch in your settings screen
func _on_analytics_toggled(on: bool) -> void:
    Ravensight.set_tracking_enabled(on)  # remembered across launches

# a "Forget me" button: a fresh random identity from now on
func _on_forget_me_pressed() -> void:
    Ravensight.reset_device_id()
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Player Reports
documents.content:
### Player Reports

 

Add an optional in-game form that captures the current game screen, lets players highlight or hide an area, and sends a short message. Bind the reporting action to a key, controller input or pause-menu button. The dashboard groups reports into issues and tracks fixes through verification.

 

Download [Ravensight.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/Ravensight.gd), [RavensightReports.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/RavensightReports.gd) and [RavensightReportOverlay.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/RavensightReportOverlay.gd). Add the latter two as children of the Ravensight autoload, named RavensightReports and ReportOverlay. Bind `ravensight_report` in Input Map. The overlay captures only the game viewport and never pauses multiplayer.

 

Reports draw from your included events and prepaid balance automatically. A text report counts as 1 event on the event meter; a screenshot adds 20,000 events to the meter, covering processing, storage and delivery. There is no separate screenshot budget to configure. Failed or canceled uploads release their reserved usage. Retention and file limits are listed in Settings. Text-only reporting remains available if capture or upload fails. Screenshots are not automatically sent to AI providers.

4. JavaScript SDK reference

 

## The ravensight package for browser games and Node

 

One zero-dependency client for browser games and Node 18 or newer, shipped as both ESM and CommonJS. It owns sessions, batching, the offline queue, rate limits and the server-side kill switch, so your game code calls `init()` once and `track()` from then on.

 

Code samples scroll horizontally when needed. Focus a sample and use the arrow keys, or swipe to read a long line.

documents.title: Install
documents.content:
### Install

 

```
npm install ravensight
```

 

There is no build step for consumers. It suits Phaser, PixiJS, three.js, Excalibur and hand-written canvas games. Godot HTML5 exports use the [Godot SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#godot-sdk) instead.

documents.content:
### Options

 

Pass these to `new Ravensight(options)`.

 

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ingestKey` | required | Your publishable `gt_live_...` key. Safe to ship in a client build. |
| `apiUrl` | `https://api.ravensight.io/api/v1` | `/api/v1` is appended if you leave it off. |
| `gameVersion` | `'1.0.0'` | Reported with the session. |
| `platform` | auto | `'web'` in a browser, `node-<platform>` in Node. |
| `autoFlushMs` | `15000` | Flush interval. `0` flushes only on demand. |
| `maxQueueSize` | `500` | Offline queue cap. The oldest events are dropped first. |
| `maxSessions` | `64` | Sessions cached at once, one per device id. The least recently used is dropped first, never the current id, and reopens on that device's next event. |
| `storage` | auto | Anything with `getItem` and `setItem`. Holds the device id. |
| `deviceId` | auto | Overrides the generated device id. |
| `enabled` | `true` | Pass `false` to start opted out. |
| `autoEvents` | `true` | Send `game_started` and `game_exited` for you, in a browser only. A client that starts with `enabled: false` sends neither. |
| `fetch` | global | Inject a custom fetch. |
| `debug` | `false` | Logs SDK activity to the console, and warns about reserved `rs_` keys. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Methods
documents.content:
### Methods

 

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `await rs.init()` | Reads the kill switch from `GET /api/v1/settings`, then opens a session. Resolves with `{ trackingEnabled, sessionReady, reason }` and never throws on a network failure. `reason` is `null` when the session is ready, otherwise one of the values in the table below. If tracking is off for your game, the queue is cleared and nothing further is sent. |
| `rs.track(event, data?, { deviceId }?)` | Queues an event and records its timestamp at the moment of the call. Safe before `init()`. Returns `false` when tracking is off. `deviceId` sends this one event as another device, under that id's own session, so one Node client can serve many players. It must be a non-empty string or `track()` throws a `TypeError`. |
| `await rs.flush()` | Sends what is queued now and resolves with `{ sent, queued }`. Concurrent calls are safe. |
| `await rs.submitFeedback(message, category?, rating?)` | Sends player feedback. `category` is one of the values below, exported as `FEEDBACK_CATEGORIES`. `rating` is an integer from 1 to 5. Leave either out with `undefined`, `null` or an empty string. Anything else is invalid and throws before any request is made, with code `invalid_category` or `invalid_rating`; an empty message throws `empty_message`. |
| `rs.setEnabled(bool)` | Local opt in and opt out. `false` stops sending and clears anything queued. The SDK does not store the choice: keep it in your own settings and call this before the first event on every launch. |
| `await rs.setDeviceId(id)` | Changes the device id, for example after a player signs in on a shared machine. The switch is immediate: nothing is flushed or waited for. The new id is stored and its session opens on the next flush. Events already queued keep the id they were tracked under and go out under that id's own session, so nothing is ever sent under the wrong id. Resolves with `{ previousId, queuedUnderPreviousId }`. Setting the current id again changes nothing. |
| `await rs.resetDeviceId()` | The same with a fresh random id, which it resolves with. Use it for a reset analytics id button. |
| `rs.joinSession(token, { deviceId }?)` | Joins a session opened elsewhere, normally the browser's `rs.sessionToken`, so the next session opened for `deviceId` (default: the client's own id) shares its analytics session. Any session already cached for that id is dropped, and the token is used once. See Joining the browser's session below. |
| `await rs.dispose({ flush = true, timeoutMs = 2000 })` | Shuts the client down and resolves with `{ sent, dropped }`. The timer and page listeners stop at once and `track()` returns `false` from that moment. The queue is then flushed by default, bounded by `timeoutMs`, even if `init()` was never called; in a browser, whatever is still queued after that goes out in one last keepalive or beacon request. Anything left is counted as dropped, and so are events in a request that timed out, even if it later lands. Pass `{ flush: false }` to discard the queue. After dispose, `setDeviceId()` and `resetDeviceId()` reject with code `disposed`. |
| `await rs.fetchSuggestions()` | Experimental. The AI-generated design suggestions for your game, empty until a weekly digest has run. The shape may change, so do not build game logic on it. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Why a session is not ready
documents.content:
### Why a session is not ready

 

| Reason | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `invalid_key` | The key was refused (`401`, or a `403` other than the kill switch). The flush timer and the automatic flush at 50 queued events stop, because retrying on a timer cannot fix a wrong key. `track()` keeps queueing up to `maxQueueSize`; `flush()` and `init()` still try again, and the first session that opens restarts the timer. |
| `tracking_disabled` | Tracking is switched off for this game. Nothing is sent. |
| `disabled` | The client is opted out (`enabled: false` or `setEnabled(false)`). `init()` makes no network call. Call `setEnabled(true)` and then `init()` to start. |
| `offline` | No answer from the network. Retried with backoff. |
| `rate_limited` | `429`. Retried after `Retry-After`. |
| `session_failed` | Any other answer. Retried with backoff. |

 

`rs.stats.lastError` holds the last failed request as `{ code, status, at }`, from the session, settings or batch requests, or `null`. Read it when events are not arriving. It can show `session_expired` after a routine `401` the SDK has already recovered from, so read it together with whether the queue is draining.

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: How delivery works
documents.content:
### How delivery works

 

- **Batches of 50.** The server's limit per request. A flush keeps sending batches until the queue drains.
 
- **Offline queue of 500.** Events wait while the network is down, up to `maxQueueSize`. Past that the oldest are dropped, so the newest are kept. An event leaves the queue when the server accepts it, or when it is dropped: a single event the server rejects with `400`, the oldest events past the queue cap, and whatever is still queued on `setEnabled(false)` or when `dispose()` finishes.
 
- **One device per batch.** Each request carries the leading run of queued events that share one device id, under that id's own session, then the next run.
 
- **401** on a batch means that device's session expired: the SDK opens a new one for that device only and sends the same batch again.
 
- **Invalid key.** A refused key stops the flush timer instead of retrying forever. Events keep queueing; `flush()` or `init()` try again.
 
- **429** honors `Retry-After`. Without that header the SDK backs off exponentially from 10 seconds up to 5 minutes. The queue is held, never discarded, though the queue cap still applies.
 
- **400** halves the batch and retries, down to a single event. An event still rejected on its own is dropped so it cannot block the rest.
 
- **Page hide.** When the page goes hidden the SDK sends one last batch, preferring `fetch` with `keepalive`. Where that is unavailable it falls back to `navigator.sendBeacon`, which cannot set headers, so the session token travels in the JSON body as `sessionToken`, never in the URL.
 
- **No re-send while in flight.** The SDK never sends a batch again while it is still in flight, so a batch cut off by a real page unload can be lost rather than counted twice. A batch whose response is lost, from a network error or a 5xx after the server already stored it, can be sent again on the next flush, and ingest does not remove duplicates.

 

Session creation and tracked events are rate limited per game, not per client. See [Usage, billing and limits](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#limits).

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: What the dashboard reads
documents.content:
### What the dashboard reads

 

The dashboard gives meaning to some fields and event names. Name your events with these in mind.

 

- **One place per event.** `level`, `location` and `track` in the event data fold into one place, and the first non-empty one wins, in that order. The level funnel, per-level deaths and journeys only see events that have a place.
 
- **Event names.** A name containing `start`, `begin` or `enter` is a level start; `complet`, `finish`, `win` or `clear` is a completion; `died`, `destroyed` or `killed` is a death. These are lowercase substring matches.
 
- **`rs_kind` overrides the name.** Set `rs_kind` in the event data to `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death` or `none` and it is read before the name. `none` opts an event out, so `checkout_started` is not a level start. An unknown value falls through to the name match. Keys that start with `rs_` are reserved for Ravensight. The SDK exports the four values as `RS_KINDS`, and with `debug: true` it warns once per event and key about an `rs_kind` outside that list or an `rs_` key Ravensight does not read. It never throws and still sends the event. The server counts the same two mistakes on the Implementation health card.
 
- **Potentially stuck** is one event repeated 10 or more times at the same level in a session of fewer than 20 events. The same event at a new level each time is movement, not stuck. Events with no place are grouped together, so ten repeats of a placeless event in a short session count; send a place or accept it.

 

```
rs.track('boss_phase_begin', { level: 'castle', rs_kind: 'none' });
rs.track('run_over', { level: 'castle', rs_kind: 'death' });
```

 

The full rules, including the player flags, are in [how the built-in detections read your events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#detection-rules).

### Privacy

 

The SDK generates a random device id and stores it under `ravensight_device_id`. It collects no hardware identifier, advertising id or personal data, only the events you send. If you pass your own `deviceId`, as on a server, make it a pseudonymous player id your game generates, never an email or account name. The row by row answers for the App Store and Google Play forms are in [what your privacy label can say](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#privacy-label).

5. LÖVE SDK reference

 

## The ravensight folder for LÖVE games

 

Pure Lua for LÖVE 11.x and 12.x on Windows, macOS and Linux. It owns the device id, sessions, batching, retries and the offline queue, and it sends requests from a background thread, so a slow network never costs a frame. There are no native files to bundle, sign or notarize.

 

Code samples scroll horizontally when needed. Focus a sample and use the arrow keys, or swipe to read a long line.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Install
documents.content:
### Install

 

Copy the `ravensight` folder from [ravensight-love](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-love) into your game, next to `main.lua`. It can live in a subfolder too (`lib/ravensight`); require it by that path. The same files are published here: [init.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/init.lua), [core.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/core.lua), [json.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/json.lua), [transport.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/transport.lua), [web.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/web.lua) and [worker.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/worker.lua), the love.js bridge [ravensight-love-bridge.js](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/ravensight-love-bridge.js) (only for a web build, it goes on the page, not in the game), the [README](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/README.md) and the [MIT license](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/LICENSE).

 

```
my-game/
  main.lua
  conf.lua
  ravensight/
    init.lua
    core.lua
    json.lua
    transport.lua
    web.lua
    worker.lua
```

 

Set an identity in `conf.lua`, so the SDK has a save folder for its device id:

 

```
function love.conf(t)
  t.identity = "my-game"
end
```

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Use
documents.content:
### Use

 

```
local ravensight = require("ravensight")

function love.load()
  ravensight.init({
    apiUrl = "https://api.ravensight.io",
    ingestKey = "gt_live_...",   -- from your game's page in the dashboard
    gameVersion = "1.0.0",
  })
end

function love.update(dt)
  ravensight.update(dt)
end

function love.quit()
  return ravensight.quit()
end

-- anywhere in your game
ravensight.track("level_start", { level = "forest_1" })
ravensight.track("level_complete", { level = "forest_1", seconds = 74, deaths = 2 })
```

 

`game_started` is sent for you on launch and `game_exited` on quit. `ravensight.quit()` returns `true` the first time, which tells LÖVE to wait while the last events are sent; the SDK quits again by itself once they are answered, or after 1.5 seconds. If your game already has a `love.quit`, return its answer from your own handler, or pass `handleQuit = false` so the SDK never delays a quit.

 

```
function love.quit()
  if not saveGame() then return true end
  return ravensight.quit()
end
```

documents.title: Options
documents.content:
### Options

 

Pass these to `ravensight.init(options)`.

 

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ingestKey` | required | Your game's publishable `gt_live_` key. Safe to ship in a build. |
| `apiUrl` | `https://api.ravensight.io` | With or without `/api/v1`. |
| `gameVersion` | `1.0.0` | Sent with every session. |
| `enabled` | `true` | `false` sends and queues nothing for this run, and is not saved. The player's opt out is `setTrackingEnabled`. |
| `maxQueueSize` | `500` | Unsent events kept. The oldest are dropped first. |
| `flushInterval` | `2` | Seconds an event waits so it can go out with others. 50 waiting events go at once. |
| `handleQuit` | `true` | Hold the quit up to 1.5 seconds to send the last events. |
| `transport` | automatic | `"https"`, `"winhttp"`, `"libcurl"` or `"curl"` to try first, or `"web"` for the love.js bridge (chosen for you in a web build). |
| `timeout` | `15` | Seconds per request. |
| `debug` | `false` | Print informational messages too. Warnings always print. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Functions
documents.content:
### Functions

 

| Function | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `track(name, data)` | Queue an event. `data` is a flat table of strings, numbers and booleans. Safe before the session is ready. |
| `flush()` | Send what is queued now. |
| `submitFeedback(message, category, rating)` | Send player feedback. `category` and `rating` (1 to 5) are optional. Needs an open session. |
| `setTrackingEnabled(enabled)` | The player's opt-out, remembered across launches. `false` drops the queue and sends nothing, not even the startup check. |
| `isTrackingEnabled()` | `false` when the player opted out or tracking is switched off for your game. |
| `resetDeviceId()` | Start a fresh analytics identity for this install. |
| `getDeviceId()` | This install's random id. |
| `getTransport()` | How requests are sent here, or `nil` if nothing works. |
| `on(event, fn)` | Listen for an SDK event. Returns a function that stops listening. |
| `update(dt)` | Call every frame. Delivers answers and runs retries. |
| `quit()` | Return it from `love.quit`. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Events
documents.content:
### Events

 

| Event | Arguments | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session_ready` | none | A session is open. |
| `session_failed` | `reason` | Opening a session failed. It is retried for you. |
| `tracking_disabled` | `source` | `"server"` when tracking is switched off for your game, `"player"` after an opt-out. |
| `events_flushed` | `count` | A batch was accepted. |
| `flush_failed` | `reason` | A batch failed. It is retried for you. |
| `feedback_submitted` | none | Feedback was accepted. |
| `feedback_failed` | `reason` | Feedback failed, including `"no_session"` when sent too early. |
| `event_tracked` | `name, data` | Every queued event, with the data actually queued. |

 

```
ravensight.on("tracking_disabled", function(source)
  print("analytics off:", source)
end)
```

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: How requests are sent
documents.content:
### How requests are sent

 

LÖVE 11 has no built-in HTTPS, and the API only accepts HTTPS, so the SDK uses the first of these that works. Nothing native is bundled.

 

1. **`require("https")`**: built into LÖVE 12, or the lua-https library if you added it to an 11.x game.
 
1. **WinHTTP** on Windows, the HTTP library every Windows version ships, called through LuaJIT's FFI.
 
1. **libcurl** on macOS and Linux, the system's own copy, through the FFI.
 
1. **The `curl` command** on macOS and Linux, if libcurl would not load.

 

If none of them works, the SDK prints one warning, keeps events queued, saves them when the game quits and tries again next launch. `getTransport()` tells you which one is in use. The libcurl and `curl` paths have been run against the live API on macOS. The WinHTTP path and Linux are written but not yet verified in a shipped build.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Delivery
documents.content:
### Delivery

 

- **Batches of 50.** Up to 50 events per request.
 
- **Backoff.** A failed request is retried after 10 seconds, doubling up to 5 minutes. A `429` with `Retry-After` is obeyed exactly.
 
- **One bad event.** If the server rejects an oversized event, the batch is split until that event is found and dropped, so it never costs the events around it.
 
- **Saved on quit.** Events still unsent when the game quits are saved in the game's save folder and sent on the next launch.
 
- **Kill switch.** If tracking is switched off for your game in the dashboard, the SDK goes quiet for the rest of the run.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Privacy and the opt-out
documents.content:
### Privacy and the opt-out

 

The SDK generates a random device id per install: 32 hex characters, a dash and the OS name, from the operating system's random source on first launch, saved in your game's save folder. It is not derived from hardware or an account, and `resetDeviceId()` replaces it. Each event carries a timestamp, your game version and the OS. There is no advertising identifier, and no field for names, emails or accounts, so a game using it needs no tracking permission prompt. The row by row store answers are in [what your privacy label can say](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#privacy-label).

 

Ravensight ships no consent screen. If your game shows one, wire it to `setTrackingEnabled(false)`, which is saved and holds across launches, and `resetDeviceId()`.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Shipping to the web
documents.content:
### Shipping to the web

 

A love.js build cannot make requests from Lua, so the page does the sending. Load the [JavaScript SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#javascript-sdk) (0.4.0 or newer) on the page and install `web/ravensight-love-bridge.js` from the repository before `Love(Module)` runs. The Lua SDK notices the web build by itself and hands every `track`, `submitFeedback`, `setTrackingEnabled` and `flush` to the page, whose SDK owns the session, the device id and the two lifecycle events. The snippet and the details are in the README's [shipping to the web](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-love#shipping-to-the-web-lovejs-itchio) section.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Not supported yet
documents.content:
### Not supported yet

 

Android and iOS are not supported yet. Ravensight Playtest has no LÖVE adapter yet; a build driven through the desktop automation server or a custom bridge reads the `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_TOKEN` and `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_RUN_ID` variables, so its persona sessions are tagged synthetic.

 

Where each SDK finds a playtest run: Godot, LÖVE, Unity (desktop), Unreal, C++ and Odin read `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_TOKEN` and `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_RUN_ID`; iOS reads them from the launch environment; Android reads the intent extras `ravensight_playtest_token` and `ravensight_playtest_run_id`; the JavaScript SDK reads the page global `__RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST__`. The table below has the other sources each one accepts.

documents.content:
6. iOS SDK reference

 

## The Ravensight Swift package for iOS and macOS

 

One Swift package for iOS 15 or newer and macOS 12 or newer, with no third party dependencies and a URLSession transport. It owns the device id, sessions, batching, the offline queue, rate limit handling and the server kill switch, and it sends player feedback and Player Reports with a screenshot.

 

Verified so far: the package's tests on macOS and on the iOS Simulator. It has not yet run inside a shipping app or on a physical device, so read the code before a release build. The source and the full README are at [ravensight-ios](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-ios). Code samples scroll horizontally when needed.

documents.section_title: The Ravensight Swift package for iOS and macOS
documents.title: Install
documents.content:
### Install

 

Swift Package Manager only. In Xcode choose File > Add Package Dependencies, paste the repository URL and add the `Ravensight` library to your app target. Or declare it in `Package.swift`:

 

```
dependencies: [
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-ios.git",
        from: "0.3.0"
    ),
],
targets: [
    .target(name: "YourGame", dependencies: ["Ravensight"]),
]
```

documents.section_title: The Ravensight Swift package for iOS and macOS
documents.title: Initialise
documents.content:
### Initialise

 

Call `start` once, early, from the main thread (your `App` init or `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)`), with the publishable `gt_live_` ingest key from the dashboard. It queues `game_started`, reads the kill switch, opens a session, sends batches every 5 seconds and hooks the app lifecycle so the queue is flushed when the player leaves.

 

```
import Ravensight

Ravensight.start(ingestKey: "gt_live_your_key")

Ravensight.track("level_completed", data: ["level": 3, "deaths": 2])

// Or the full configuration:
var configuration = RavensightConfiguration(ingestKey: "gt_live_your_key")
configuration.gameVersion = "1.2.0"
configuration.persistQueue = true
Ravensight.start(configuration)
```

 

On iOS a session ends by time in the background: a player who comes back within `sessionTimeout` (30 minutes by default) carries on the same session, and one who comes back later, or after the app was swiped away, gets the old session's `game_exited` stamped with the time they left, then a new session.

documents.title: Playtest tagging, and why a synthetic id is never mirrored
documents.content:
### Playtest tagging, and why a synthetic id is never mirrored

 

A Ravensight Playtest run identifies itself with a token and a run id, from `RavensightConfiguration.playtestToken` and `playtestRunId`, or else from the `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_TOKEN` and `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_RUN_ID` launch environment variables (on the Simulator, `xcrun simctl launch` passes a variable through when you prefix it with `SIMCTL_CHILD_`). With a token, every request carries the `X-Ravensight-Playtest` header and the run sends the device id `pt-<runId>`, held in memory only and exposed as `playtestDeviceId`. The persisted queue is not used. A token without a run id never runs as a real player: nothing is sent.

 

`Ravensight.deviceId` always returns the durable id, never the synthetic one, and `resetDeviceId()` never returns a synthetic id either, so an app that copies the id into its own storage or its own server is safe. Never copy `playtestDeviceId` anywhere that outlives the run. A mirrored `pt-` id would come back on a later launch: a real player's events would then be filed under a persona's run and left out of every report that hides playtest sessions, and your own records would count a persona as a player. `Ravensight.isSynthetic` tells you which kind of run this is. Leave the token and run id unset in a build for real players.

documents.title: The persisted queue
documents.content:
### The persisted queue

 

By default the queue lives in memory, so events still queued when the process dies are lost. With `persistQueue = true` the queue is mirrored to one JSON file under Application Support, excluded from backups: at most the newest 500 events, written atomically whenever the queue changes and read when the client is created. Restored events keep their original timestamps, and events older than 89 days are not restored. The file is deleted on an opt-out, on `stopAllTelemetry`, on `resetDeviceId`, on the kill switch and when the queue drains, and a playtest run never reads or writes it. It narrows the window in which events can be lost; an event tracked a moment before a crash may not have been written yet.

documents.content:
7. HTTP API

 

## Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot

 

Building for the web or Node? The [JavaScript SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#javascript-sdk) wraps everything below in a zero-dependency client with batching, an offline queue, and tab-close flushing. Unity developers use the [Unity SDK](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unity), and LÖVE games use the [LÖVE SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#love-sdk). Everything else speaks plain HTTP.

 

The Godot SDK is a client for this same surface. If you're on Unity, Unreal, a browser game, or anything else, this is what to call directly. The ingest endpoints answer any web origin, so browser games on GitHub Pages, itch.io or your own site need no CORS setup.

 

Base URL

 

```
https://api.ravensight.io
```

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/session
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/session

 

Opens a session for a device. Auth: `X-API-Key` (your ingest key). The game identity comes from the key, never from the body.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/session
X-API-Key: gt_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "deviceId": "3f9ac2e17b5d4c0e8a61f2b9d7c04e5a-windows",
  "gameVersion": "1.4.2",
  "platform": "Windows"
}
```

 

Response, 201

 

```
{
  "token": "st_9f2c...redacted",
  "expiresAt": "2026-08-29T16:00:00.000Z",
  "expiresIn": 86400
}
```

 

Errors: `400 missing_device_id` when `deviceId` is absent, `401 invalid_api_key` or `missing_api_key`, `403 tracking_disabled` when the game's kill switch is off, `429 rate_limited` at more than 60 session creations per minute for the game.

 

**Joining a session.** Send `joinToken`, the token of a live session from the same game, instead of a `deviceId`, and the new session shares that session's analytics session id and device id. Use it when a second client of the same player, such as your game server, should report into the player's session. The new session keeps its own `platform` and `gameVersion`, never outlives the one it joined, and the answer has the same shape. A `deviceId` in the same body never becomes the new session's device id. A join from a synthetic (playtest) session stays synthetic: the new session belongs to the same run, its events are marked synthetic and are never metered, and feedback sent through it is marked synthetic too. It keeps the playtest's own platform whatever the body says, and once the run or its job has finished, its events and feedback answer `403 playtest_job_closed`. When a join from a synthetic session also sends the player's own `deviceId`, that device's real sessions in the same game from the last 15 minutes join the run too, their events are marked synthetic, and the answer adds `adopted` with how many. Events they sent before the join were already counted on the event meter and are not refunded, so have your game server open its session with the browser's session token as `joinToken` before it tracks the sign-up, and nothing is tracked as real first.

 

```
{
  "joinToken": "st_9f2c...redacted",
  "gameVersion": "1.4.2",
  "platform": "dedicated-server"
}
```

 

A token that is unknown, expired, revoked, from another game, or from a doctor session answers `401 invalid_join_token`, the same answer for each, so a token's existence never leaks; so does a join sent with `"platform": "doctor"` or a playtest header. A `platform` or `gameVersion` that is not a string answers `400 invalid_platform` or `invalid_game_version`. Joins count toward the same 60 a minute.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/track
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/track

 

Sends a single event. Auth: `X-Session-Token` (from step above).

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/track
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "event": "level_completed",
  "data": { "level": 3, "score": 15000, "time_seconds": 87.4 },
  "timestamp": <unix seconds, within the last 90 days>
}
```

 

Response, 202

 

```
{ "accepted": 1 }
```

 

`timestamp` is optional, in unix seconds, and defaults to the time the server receives the event. An event whose timestamp is more than 90 days old is dropped: it is not stored and not charged, and it is counted as `timestamp_too_old` on the Implementation health card. The request still succeeds, so `accepted` can be lower than the number of events you sent, on this endpoint and on `/track/batch`.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/track/batch
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/track/batch

 

Sends up to 50 events in one call. Same auth as `/track`.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/track/batch
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "events": [
    { "event": "level_started", "data": { "level": 3 } },
    { "event": "checkpoint_reached", "data": { "idx": 2 } }
  ]
}
```

 

Response, 202

 

```
{ "accepted": 2 }
```

 

Errors: `400 invalid_batch` when `events` is missing or empty, `400 batch_too_large` above 50 events, `400 missing_event` if any entry lacks an `event` name.

 

Keys that start with `rs_` in event data are reserved. An `rs_kind` that is not `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death` or `none`, and any other `rs_` key Ravensight does not read, is stored as sent and counted as `rs_kind_unknown` or `rs_key_unknown` on the Implementation health card.

 

**What the dashboard reads from your events.** `level`, `location` and `track` in `data` fold into one place, and the first non-empty one wins. The level funnel counts three kinds at a place: `level_start`, `level_complete` and `death`. Set `rs_kind` to say which one an event is; without it the kind is read from the event name. An event with a place and none of those kinds is shown as navigation only, stays out of the funnel, and is counted as `place_without_kind` on the Implementation health card. Send `rs_kind: "none"` when the place is intentional. The full rules are in [how the built-in detections read your events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#detection-rules).

### GET /api/v1/agent/suggestions

 

Experimental, machine-readable design suggestions from your weekly digest. Auth: `X-API-Key`. Returns an empty array until a digest has run for your game.

 

```
{ "suggestions": [] }
```

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: GET /api/v1/doctor/ping/:nonce
documents.content:
### GET /api/v1/doctor/ping/:nonce

 

The read-back for [the doctor's live check](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#doctor). Auth: `X-API-Key`. A session opened with `"platform": "doctor"` lives ten minutes, gets a device id the server chooses, and may send only `ravensight_doctor_ping`, ten a minute per game (`400 doctor_event_only` for any other name, and for feedback and player reports). Its events are kept out of your analytics and your event usage. This endpoint answers whether the ping whose `rs_doctor` value is `:nonce`, 32 lowercase hex characters, was stored for the key's game in the last 15 minutes.

 

Response, 200

 

```
{ "found": true, "acceptedAt": "2026-10-10T12:00:01.250Z" }
```

 

`404 {"found": false, "error": "ping_not_found"}` until the event is stored, which can take a few seconds while it is batched. `400 invalid_nonce` for a malformed nonce, `429 rate_limited` above 30 reads a minute for the game, `503 storage_unavailable` when event storage is down. A nonce sent by another game reads as not found.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/feedback
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/feedback

 

Auth: `X-Session-Token`.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/feedback
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "message": "Level 3's second checkpoint feels unfair.",
  "category": "suggestion",
  "rating": 4
}
```

 

Response, 201

 

```
{ "id": "66c1f2a9d4e8b0021f9a7c31" }
```

 

`category` and `rating` are both optional. When present, `category` must be one of `bug`, `suggestion`, `complaint`, `praise`, `playtest`, or `other`.

documents.title: Errors
documents.content:
### Errors

 

| Status | Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `missing_device_id`, `missing_event`, `invalid_batch`, `batch_too_large`, `event_name_too_long`, `event_too_large`, `invalid_event_data`, `missing_message`, `message_too_long`, `invalid_category`, `invalid_feedback`, `doctor_event_only`, `invalid_nonce`, `invalid_platform`, `invalid_game_version` | Malformed request body or a payload ceiling (see Limits). |
| 401 | `missing_api_key`, `invalid_api_key`, `invalid_join_token`, or a missing/expired session token | Bad or absent credentials for the header the endpoint expects, or a `joinToken` that cannot be joined. |
| 404 | `ping_not_found` | The doctor's ping is not stored yet, or was never sent for this game. Only returned by `GET /api/v1/doctor/ping/:nonce`. |

| 429 | `quota_exceeded` | Monthly event quota reached for this account. Carries a `Retry-After` header, in seconds until the quota resets at the next UTC month. |
| 503 | `storage_unavailable` | Event storage is temporarily unavailable. Carries `Retry-After: 60`; nothing was accepted or charged against quota. |

documents.content:
8. Projects and environments

 

## One title, one project, one game per environment

 

Your development build and your shipped build must not share an event stream, or a week of debugging quietly becomes your retention number. Ravensight keeps them apart by making each one its own game, and groups the games of one title into a project.

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: The three scopes
documents.content:
### The three scopes

 

| Scope | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| Environment, one game | Its own ingest key, its own tracking and history switches, and its own events, sessions, players, funnels, journeys, retention, reports and digests. Labels are fixed: production, staging, development, at most one of each per project. |
| Project, one title | Name and engine, and the environments underneath it. Project-scoped pages read the project rather than one build. |
| Studio, your org | Members and roles, billing and the prepaid balance, the studio context graph, studio notes, cross-game analytics and the audit log. |

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: Picking one
documents.content:
### Picking one

 

The switcher at the top of the sidebar picks a project. Beside it in the header, on the pages whose numbers come from one build, an environment control picks which environment you are looking at. A project with a single environment needs no second choice, and the pages that belong to the whole project do not show the control at all.

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: Managing them
documents.content:
### Managing them

 

**Settings > Projects** is where projects are renamed, merged, and given new environments. Because every existing game was migrated into a project of its own, two environments of the same title can start out as two projects. Ravensight proposes the merge when their names normalize to the same thing and their environment labels do not collide, and nothing is merged until you accept the proposal. Dismiss one and it stays dismissed. You can also move a single environment from one project to another, or delete a project once it is empty.

 

Creating, renaming, merging and deleting all need an admin role or above. Everyone in the studio can read the list.

 

Analytics queries are still keyed on one game, which is why a number on screen always belongs to exactly one environment. A project-level or studio-level number is the same per-game query asked of several games and summed, never a new aggregation with its own rules.
